nameStory: The "water flea" gets its name from its jerky, hopping swimming style that resembles a flea bouncing through the water. Despite the name, these tiny creatures aren't fleas at all - they're actually small crustaceans related to shrimp and crabs! The scientific name Daphnia comes from a Greek water nymph, fitting for these graceful aquatic dancers.
description: The Common Water Flea is a tiny freshwater crustacean about the size of a pinhead, typically measuring 1-3 millimeters long. These translucent little animals have a distinctive bean-shaped body enclosed in a clear shell, with a prominent black eye that's easily visible even without magnification. They swim with a distinctive jerky motion using their large, feathery antennae like oars. You'll often see them carrying bright green or orange eggs in a special pouch, making them look like tiny living jewels in the water.

idTips.label: Jerky Swimming Motion
idTips.description: Watch for their characteristic hop-and-glide swimming pattern as they use their large antennae to propel through the water in short bursts

idTips.label: Single Black Eye
idTips.description: Look for one prominent dark eye spot that's clearly visible even in these tiny creatures - it stands out like a black dot against their translucent body

idTips.label: Transparent Bean Shape
idTips.description: The body appears as a clear, oval shell that you can see through, often revealing internal organs as dark shadows

idTips.label: Feathery Antennae
idTips.description: Two large, branched antennae extend from the head like tiny feathers and beat rhythmically to propel them through water

idTips.label: Egg Pouch
idTips.description: Females often carry a visible brood pouch filled with bright green or orange eggs that looks like a colorful backpack

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of a pinhead or small grain of sand - visible to the naked eye but details require magnification

habitat: Common Water Fleas live in still or slow-moving freshwater throughout New England, including ponds, lakes, temporary pools, and quiet backwaters of streams. They prefer nutrient-rich waters and are especially abundant in shallow areas with plenty of algae and organic matter to feed on. You'll find them in everything from farm ponds to woodland pools, often in massive numbers during population booms.

seasonality.spring: Populations explode as waters warm, with females reproducing rapidly through parthenogenesis (cloning themselves). This is peak viewing time as their numbers can make water appear cloudy.
seasonality.summer: Remain active and visible, though hot weather may drive them deeper. Look for them in early morning or evening in shallower waters.
seasonality.fall: Begin producing winter eggs as temperatures drop. Females may appear more orange or reddish due to special winter egg production.
seasonality.winter: Most adults die off, but hardy winter eggs survive frozen in pond sediments, waiting for spring warmth to hatch the next generation.

funFact: Daphnia pulex was the first crustacean to have its entire genome sequenced, and scientists discovered it has more genes than humans do - about 31,000 compared to our 20,000-25,000!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Daphnia species, but the Common Water Flea tends to be slightly larger and more abundant than its relatives. The key is the combination of size, the single prominent eye, and that distinctive jerky swimming motion - other tiny freshwater creatures like copepods swim more smoothly.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "fleas," these are crustaceans in the same group as lobsters and crabs, not insects. They're often called "indicator species" by scientists because they're sensitive to water pollution, so healthy water flea populations usually mean clean water.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Daphnia mendotae, the Common Water Flea is generally more robust and adaptable to different water conditions. While both species look very similar under casual observation, D. pulex tends to be slightly larger and more commonly found in smaller, temporary water bodies, whereas D. mendotae prefers larger, permanent lakes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Daphnia mendotae is distinguished from the more common Daphnia pulex primarily by its habitat preferences and slightly smaller size.
